The silky cuscus, Phalanger sericeus, is a montane possum inhabiting the highland forests of New Guinea, where environmental temperatures can be quite cool. Resting metabolic rate measurements, taken from individuals acclimated to laboratory conditions, indicate a basal oxygen consumption of 428.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 428.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the ambient temperature was held at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This relatively elevated metabolic output is typical for arboreal folivores that must maintain core body temperature in a cool, wet montane habitat. Comparative physiological studies with congeneric species reveal that this value aligns closely with the allometric expectations for a marsupial of its size, suggesting that the silky cuscus does not exhibit pronounced metabolic depression despite its sluggish, arboreal lifestyle. Such data provide a critical baseline for understanding the energetic constraints faced by this species in its native environment.

Neonatal mass is an exceedingly challenging parameter to measure directly in wild marsupials, and for the silky cuscus no direct field data exist. Based on the well-documented birth weight of the closely related spotted cuscus, Spilocuscus maculatus, the wet mass of a newborn silky cuscus is estimated at approximately 0.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.9 grams]. Such a minuscule neonate, typical of many arboreal phalangerids, is born after a remarkably brief gestation. The gestation period has been inferred from the better-known life history of the northern common cuscus, Phalanger orientalis, and is thought to last 13 days [tg = 13 days] at a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. After this short internal development, the altricial newborn must crawl to the pouch and attach to a teat for an extended period of postnatal development.

The developmental trajectory following birth proceeds through several well-defined life stages. Under standard thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence from milk, is estimated to occur at 270 days since birth [tx = 270 days since birth]. This relatively prolonged period of maternal investment is characteristic of marsupials, during which the offspring completes much of its somatic growth while attached to the teat within the pouch. Following weaning, the growing juvenile continues to mature, reaching sexual maturity at approximately 300 days since birth [tp = approximately 300 days since birth] when maintained at the same at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]thermal regime. These developmental benchmarks were derived by extrapolating from detailed life-history studies on Spilocuscus maculatus, a larger-bodied but ecologically analogous phalangerid.

Adult female silky cuscuses exhibit a moderate degree of sexual size dimorphism, with mature individuals attaining a maximum adult body weight in the range of 1.7 to 2.4 kilograms. The ultimate wet weight for females has been recorded at 2300 grams [Wwi = 2300 grams], representing the upper limit of typical body mass for this species. This size, combined with its folivorous diet and relatively slow metabolism, places the silky cuscus squarely within the energetic profile expected for a medium-sized arboreal marsupial. The reproductive output is correspondingly low, consistent with a strategy of producing a single, well-provisioned offspring annually. Under the standard thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], females give birth to one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] and produce just one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], a pattern that reflects the extended period of lactation and maternal care required.

Lifespan estimates for the silky cuscus are largely derived from captive records of the spotted cuscus, Spilocuscus maculatus, as no long-term field studies have been conducted on Phalanger sericeus itself. The oldest documented individuals in captivity have survived for approximately 18.9 years [am = approximately 18.9 years] under the standard thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This impressive longevity for a marsupial of its size likely reflects a slow-paced life history characterized by delayed reproduction, low reproductive output, and extended parental care. In combination with the species’ low annual fecundity and the substantial developmental period required for the offspring to reach nutritional and reproductive independence, this extended lifespan underscores a classic bet-hedging strategy adapted to the unpredictable resource availability of montane New Guinea forests.
